name: Basic Hand Tools (Hammer, Chisel, Saw)
tagline: Percussion, cutting, and ripping tools that convert human intent into shaped wood, stone, and metal
problem:
The physical human body is severely constrained in its raw mechanical interactions with the environment: human hands lack the shear strength to tear seasoned timber, the point pressure to cleave metamorphic stone, and the concentrated hardness to fracture or shear metallurgy. Without mechanical amplification, shaping raw organic and mineral matter into shelter, vessels, machines, or infrastructure is physically impossible or restricted to glacial abrasion rates.

Every primary transformation of matter requires focusing human kinetic energy into defined vector geometries. Striking requires impulse concentration (integral of force over dwell time) delivered over sub-millisecond durations to initiate brittle fracture or plastic deformation. Cutting and paring require advancing a microscopic wedge profile through cellular lignified matrix at acute shear angles without crushing surrounding fibers. Sawing requires continuous progressive chip evacuation along an alternating kerf channel without thermal binding or blade bucking.

The challenge of hand tool technology is not merely possessing a sharp or heavy object, but mastering the tribology, metallurgy, ergonomics, and structural dynamics that allow human muscle power to execute thousands of repetitive high-energy cycles without tool failure, self-injury, or rapid degradation. Furthermore, hand tools represent the absolute bootstrap foundation of all subsequent industrial technology: every lathe, mill, dynamo, engine, and semiconductor foundry is constructed using machine tools that were originally built, calibrated, and aligned using hand scrapers, chisels, hammers, and files.

In emergency survival, deep-field recovery, and space habitat expeditionary settings, basic non-powered hand tools represent the ultimate unjammable infrastructure. When power grids collapse, liquid fuel spoils, or microchips fry from electromagnetic pulses, precision hand tools convert human biological calories directly into reconstructed physical reality.
overview:
Basic hand tools represent humanity foundational suite of mechanical transducers: levers, wedges, and kinetic impulse multipliers that allow manual labor to accurately deform, cleave, and shape solid matter. The core triad comprises percussion tools (hammers, mallets), cleaving/paring tools (chisels, adzes, drawknives), and tensioned reciprocating chip-forming tools (saws, rasps).

1. Hammers and Percussion: A hammer converts rotational arm kinematics into concentrated linear kinetic energy (0.5 * m * v^2). Striking face geometry dictates impulse characteristics: crowned spherical faces prevent perimeter gouging, while hardened flat faces maximize shock transfer. Striking tools require differential heat treatment: the face must be tempered to 50-55 HRC to resist deformation, while the eye must remain soft and tough (30-35 HRC) to absorb shock without brittle catastrophic fragmentation. Ash, hickory, or spotted gum hafts provide anisotropic fiber orientation that dampens acoustic and kinetic shock waves before reaching the operator elbow.

2. Chisels and Wedges: Chisels utilize acute inclined planes to exceed the ultimate shear strength of wood or the yield strength of cold annealed metal. Wood chisels utilize primary grinding angles of 25 degrees for paring softwood up to 30 degrees for heavy mortise chopping, backed by a micro-bevel honed to sub-micron polish on abrasive waterstones. Cold chisels for metallurgy employ a robust 60-degree included angle hardened to 58 HRC with a softer striking butt that must be frequently dressed to prevent deadly mushrooming spall.

3. Saws and Progressive Evacuation: A saw is an array of microscopic chisels mounted on a spring-tempered steel plate (45-48 HRC). Rip saws feature forward-raked 60-degree triangular teeth that chisel out end-grain fibers in long chips. Crosscut saws feature knife-beveled teeth angled at 45 degrees to sever cellular walls on both sides of the kerf before clearing the central waste. Alternating tooth set bends adjacent teeth outwards by 0.2-0.4 mm, creating a cutting path wider than the saw blade body to prevent friction binding and thermal expansion warping.

4. Maintenance and Ergonomics: Tool longevity and safety depend strictly on systematic dressing. Grinding burns must be rigorously avoided, as thermal spikes above 200 degrees Celsius ruin the temper of high-carbon tool steel. Hafts must be seated with dry hardwood wedges followed by diagonal cross-wedges to ensure total radial compression within the eye.

principles.name: Impulse and momentum
principles.explanation: Hammer blow efficacy depends on momentum at impact; elastic rebound wastes energy unless managed (e.g., dead-blow fillers).

principles.name: Wedge action
principles.explanation: Chisels and axes concentrate force along a line, driving cracks along grain or shear planes in metal swarf.

principles.name: Cutting geometry
principles.explanation: Positive rake slices; negative rake scrapes. Tooth geometry must match fibre orientation — rip teeth act like chisels; crosscut teeth shear fibres.

principles.name: Stress risers
principles.explanation: Square corners at hammer eyes or chisel sockets initiate cracks; rounding and gradual tapers improve fatigue life.

components.name: Hammer head
components.function: Delivers impact; may include pein or claw
components.madeFrom: Wrought iron, steel, stone maul prehistoric
components.criticalNote: Secure wedge pin — loose heads are projectiles

components.name: Handle (haft)
components.function: Provides lever arm and shock damping via flex
components.criticalNote: Grain runout at eye equals failure

components.name: Chisel blade
components.function: Cuts wood or metal by shearing and wedging
components.madeFrom: Hardened steel edge welded to softer body in quality tools
components.criticalNote: Do not use sideways pry loads — snaps tang

components.name: Saw plate and teeth
components.position: Tensioned in frame (frame saw) or handheld
components.criticalNote: Rust increases binding — oil lightly, not sticky

components.name: Use-case boundary
components.function: Defines what Basic Hand Tools (Hammer, Chisel, Saw) is meant to accomplish and what it must not be used for
components.madeFrom: Written requirements, hazard notes, local constraints, and responsible operator assignment
components.criticalNote: A vague use case leads to unsafe improvisation.

buildSteps.title: Forge or grind hammer head blank
buildSteps.description: Upset stock to mass; punch eye hot; drift to final eye size parallel to striking face. Dress faces flat and perpendicular to eye axis.

buildSteps.title: Fit handle with interference and wedge
buildSteps.description: Burn handle in slightly oversize eye; trim shoulder seat; drive wooden wedge across grain; add steel wedge if needed.
buildSteps.warningNote: Loose handle after first day of use — re-wedge before next swing

buildSteps.title: Grind and heat-treat chisel
buildSteps.description: Normalize, harden edge zone, temper back for toughness. Flatten back; hone bevel at consistent angle.
buildSteps.warningNote: Overhard chisels chip on knot impacts

buildSteps.title: Shape and sharpen saw teeth
buildSteps.description: Joint teeth level; file rip or crosscut profiles; set teeth with saw set tool; test cut in scrap matching work species.
buildSteps.warningNote: Dull saws require excess force — primary kickback cause

buildSteps.title: Proof and maintain
buildSteps.description: Strike cold chisels only with appropriate hammer faces; peen hammer handle swell if loose; store saws dry and lightly oiled.
buildSteps.warningNote: Never use a claw hammer on hardened steel tools — face chips become shrapnel

history.event: Ground stone axes and adzes precede metal, establishing hafting and edge maintenance cultures.
Metal axes, chisels, and saws appear in carpentry contexts with preserved timber joinery.
Mass-produced crucible-steel chisels and spring-steel saws spread through building trades as industrial toolmaking standardises alloys and heat treatment.

impact: Hand tools are the debugger of civilisation: when power fails, roads crack, or factories stop, chisels and saws still modify reality. They are also pedagogical — teaching grain, hardness, and human factors before anyone touches a lathe.

warnings: High-velocity metal spall hazard: Striking two hardened tool faces together (e.g., hardened hammer face directly against another hammer or non-dressed chisel head) causes catastrophic micro-fracture emitting supersonic steel shrapnel; always wear impact-rated eye protection and regularly file off mushroomed edges.

Laceration and severe neurovascular damage: Always clamp workpieces rigidly with bench dogs, wedges, or vises; keep the non-dominant guide hand strictly behind or laterally offset from the cutting edge vector at all times.

Catastrophic haft failure: Inspect wooden tool handles for longitudinal grain runout, loose wedges, or dry rot prior to every work shift; never repair cracked or split tool handles with tape, wire, or adhesive - replace the haft entirely.

Repetitive strain and vibration syndrome: Striking mechanics must rely on rhythmic elbow, shoulder, and torso flexure rather than rigid wrist lock; damp vibration using resilient wooden hafts and rubberized leather wraps.
